blocks.text: Design Focus Area: Medication Management and Reminder Systems

A major challenge faced by many people is managing their daily medication schedules accurately and consistently. Individuals who take multiple medicines each day often struggle to remember the correct timing, dosage, and sequence of tablets. This issue is particularly common among elderly users, patients with chronic illnesses, and individuals with busy lifestyles.

Missing medication or taking it at the wrong time can reduce the effectiveness of treatment and may lead to serious health complications. Users may accidentally skip doses, take duplicate doses, or confuse medicines that look similar. Traditional storage methods such as pill boxes and medicine packets help organise medication but do not actively remind users when to take their medicines or help prevent mistakes.

Many people currently rely on phone alarms, written notes, or memory alone to manage their medication schedules. However, these methods are not always reliable, especially for users with hearing difficulties, memory decline, or complex medication routines. As healthcare becomes increasingly dependent on technology, there is a growing need for smarter systems that can improve medication organisation, reduce human error, and provide clear and accessible reminders.
Why Is This Area Important?

Taking medication correctly is an essential part of maintaining health and managing long-term medical conditions. Research from the NHS indicates that many people miss doses because they forget, become distracted, or do not have a reminder system that suits their lifestyle. This challenge becomes greater for older adults, who may experience memory decline, reduced hearing, or more complex prescription schedules.

A 2024 review of medication dispensing and reminder systems examined 426 studies and selected 56 for detailed analysis. The large volume of research highlights the significance of medication adherence as a global healthcare issue. The findings suggest that improving medication management remains an important opportunity for designers and engineers to develop solutions that support users in their daily lives.

Furthermore, increasing life expectancy and the growing number of people living with chronic illnesses mean that more individuals are required to manage multiple medications over long periods. This increases the need for reliable systems that can support users and reduce medication-related errors.
Consequences of Medication Non-Adherence
Medication non-adherence can have serious effects on both individuals and society.
Medical Consequences

Missing doses may cause treatments to become less effective and can lead to the worsening of chronic conditions such as diabetes, heart disease, or high blood pressure. In some cases, incorrect medication use can result in medical emergencies or hospitalisation.
Economic Consequences

Medication-related mistakes contribute to unnecessary healthcare costs through additional doctor visits, emergency treatment, hospital admissions, and wasted medication. These costs place additional pressure on healthcare systems.
Social and Caregiver Consequences

Family members and caregivers often play an important role in helping individuals manage medication schedules. Constant monitoring can create stress, anxiety, and caregiver burnout, particularly when supporting elderly patients or individuals with multiple prescriptions. Improving medication management can help reduce this burden and promote greater independence for users.
The Issue with Existing Solutions

Although traditional pill boxes are widely used, they are passive systems that only organise medication. They do not remind users when medication is due, confirm whether medication has been taken, or prevent accidental mistakes.

Similarly, phone alarms and written reminders can be ignored, forgotten, or switched off without action being taken. Users may still struggle to identify the correct medication, particularly when several tablets look similar. These limitations make current solutions less effective for individuals with complex medication schedules.

While advanced smart medication dispensers are available on the market, many of these products are expensive and may not be affordable for all users. Some systems also require subscription services, internet connectivity, or complex setup procedures, which can discourage elderly users and those with limited technical knowledge. As a result, many people continue to rely on basic reminder methods that do not adequately support medication management.

Therefore, there is a need for a medication management system that is affordable, easy to use, and capable of actively assisting users through clear reminders, medication identification, and controlled dispensing. Such a system could help improve medication adherence while remaining accessible to a wider range of users.

Secondary Research
Common causes of missed medication
Forgetting the exact time of a dose, especially when daily routines are busy or irregular.
Confusing one medicine with another when several tablets look similar or are taken at different times.
Taking medicine late, early, or twice because there is no clear record of whether a dose was already taken.
Depending only on memory or a single alarm, which is often not enough for people with multiple medicines.
Having difficulty reading labels or hearing alerts, which can affect older users and people with accessibility needs.

The NHS guidance also says that people often respond better when medicine-taking is linked to everyday activities such as meals, brushing teeth, or other regular habits. That suggests timing alone is not always enough, and reminders may work better when they connect to a routine the user already knows.
Evidence from studies

A medicine reminder system study tested a microcontroller-based device with 110 patients and found that 84% said it reminded them effectively at the correct time. The same system used an RTC, OLED display, buzzer, vibration, and phone calls, showing that multiple reminder methods can work together better than one method alone. This is useful evidence because it shows that visual, sound, and mobile alerts are practical in real use.

The NHS SPS guidance says that text or telephone reminders may be more effective when they are personal or interactive, but electronic drug monitors on their own are unlikely to improve adherence without extra support. That is important because it suggests that a reminder system should not only alert the user, but should also support behavior and follow-up. The same source also states that some programmable dispensers can help, but they may be too complex for some users and need careful suitability testing.

A 2024 study on older adults reports that around 50% of older adults struggle with medication adherence. That figure is useful because it shows the problem is not rare or minor. It also supports focusing on older users as a key group when developing a design idea.
Older adults as users

Older adults are a strong user group for this topic because they are more likely to take multiple medications and may need support remembering schedules. The research indicates that reminder systems for older adults need to be simple, clear, and not overly technical. If a system is too complex to set up or refill, it may not be used consistently.

A descriptive study on pillboxes found that 85% of older adults said the pillbox helped them manage their medicines. This is useful because it shows organized storage itself has value, even before electronics are added. However, a pillbox mainly helps with organization; it does not automatically remind users or track whether a dose was taken.
Related Studies(The information below until the references are from a research paper)

Recent studies have explored different methods to improve medication adherence among patients. One study by [6] examined the effectiveness of using customized Short Messaging Service (SMS) reminders through mobile technology. Conducted in resource-poor areas of Pakistan with 200 participants, the study found that patients who received personalized medication reminders and health-related SMS messages showed better medication adherence and lower average diastolic blood pressure compared to those who only received regular care.

Similarly, [1] carried out a systematic review to evaluate the impact of text messaging on treatment adherence among patients with arterial occlusive diseases. The review included seven trials involving 1,310 participants. However, the researchers concluded that there was insufficient evidence to confirm the effectiveness of text-message interventions due to the very low quality of available evidence. They emphasized the need for more reliable randomized trials, especially in low- and middle-income countries.

Another study by [3] investigated the effectiveness of low-cost medication reminder devices in improving adherence. The study involved 53,480 participants who were taking one to three long-term oral medications and were not consistently following their prescribed treatment plans. Participants were divided into groups based on whether they were taking medication for cardiovascular or other chronic conditions, or antidepressants. They were then randomly assigned to use reminder tools such as pill bottle strips with toggles, digital timer caps, or standard pillboxes, while another group received no reminder device and served as the control group.

In Viet Nam, [4] conducted a formative study on the use of the Wisepill evriMED Medication Event Reminder Monitor (MERM).  among patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in Thanh Hoa province. Twenty patients participated in the randomized controlled trial. Half of them received daily reminder alerts and scheduled reviews of their dosing history, while the remaining participants used the device without alerts. Researchers later conducted in-depth interviews to understand the patients’ experiences and opinions about the system.

The importance of mobile phone usage in supporting public health programs in low- and middle-income countries was also highlighted in a study by [8]. The researchers evaluated a two-way SMS reminder system called Zindagi SMS to determine its impact on tuberculosis treatment success in Karachi, Pakistan. The randomized controlled trial involved 2,207 participants who were assigned either to the Zindagi SMS intervention group or to a control group. The main outcome measured was the rate of successful treatment completion recorded clinically.

Another related study by [5] focused on the development of a smartphone-based medication self-management system (SMSS). The researchers designed and tested the feasibility of the system using feedback collected from interviews with 116 patients. The SMSS provided two main features through smartphones: maintaining accurate medication histories and records, and sending reminders whenever patients forgot to take their medication.

Although SMS-based reminder systems have shown effectiveness, they still present several limitations. One major challenge is the cost of sending multiple SMS reminders daily. For patients who require reminders several times a day, the monthly expense from mobile network providers can become significant. In addition, if the device runs out of credit, reminders may not be delivered. Another issue is that patients may fail to notice the alert if they are not near their phones at the time the message arrives.

To address these limitations, this project proposes the use of phone calls instead of SMS as a medication reminder method. This approach improves upon the work of [10] and is expected to be both more cost-effective and more reliable, since phone call ringing durations are generally longer and harder to ignore than SMS notifications.

The proposed system will also allow users to provide the contact details of a dedicated medical staff member who can be notified if the patient fails to respond to reminders. This feature extends the work of [2], which integrated prescription schedules into medication reminder systems. Furthermore, the system will include a vibration feature alongside audio notifications, providing an alternative alert method for physically challenged patients who may have difficulty hearing voice reminders.

Reminder methods
Audio reminders
Audio reminders are useful because they can get attention even when the user is not looking at a screen.
Studies and NHS guidance suggest that audible reminders are helpful for many users, especially when combined with other cues.
Loud or sudden alarms can be unsuitable for some users, so the tone and volume matter.
Visual reminders
OLED or screen-based reminders can show the medicine name, time, or dose in a readable format.
Visual alerts help users who may have hearing difficulties or who need confirmation before taking medicine.
The NHS notes that better reminder charts and visible prompts can be practical and cost-effective.
Vibrating reminders
Vibrating alerts are used for people with hearing impairments or for situations where sound is not ideal.
The NHS specifically mentions that audible/vibrating alarms may benefit the hearing impaired.
This is a good example of designing for different user needs rather than assuming one alert style fits everyone.
Mobile reminders
Text or phone reminders can support users when they are away from the medicine storage area.
The NHS says these are most effective when they are personal or interactive.
Research also suggests that app-based reminders need backup features and caregiver support to be more reliable.
Storage and dispensing

The systematic review on pill and medication dispensers describes many devices that open sections at set times, often with alarms. It notes that these systems may suit patients with stable but somewhat complex medication regimens. This is especially relevant because multiple daily medicines often need both storage and timing support.

The review also shows that a major challenge is making sure the correct medicine is presented at the correct time without creating confusion. Some devices are useful but complex to fill, which can be a problem for older adults or caregivers. That means future designs should aim to be easy to load, easy to read, and difficult to misuse.

The same review highlights remote monitoring and caregiver alerts as useful directions in this area. That shows the research is moving from simple reminder tools toward systems that also support supervision and accountability. This gradual development helps build the case for a more interactive medication management product.
What users still struggle with :
They may remember the reminder but still forget whether they actually took the dose.
They may ignore a reminder if it is too generic, too frequent, or poorly timed.
They may get confused if several medicines are scheduled close together.
They may find complex dispenser systems difficult to refill or set up.
They may need support from family or caregivers to stay consistent.
Conclusion :

The research suggests that no single method solves every medication problem. That is why systems are increasingly combining storage, reminders, and confirmation features rather than using only one function.
Additional evidence on the scale of the problem

A 2025/2026 study of 42,601 older adult records found medication non-adherence of 5.9%, and it linked the issue mainly to pharmacological factors, inappropriate use, and multiple chronic conditions with multiple medication regimens. This is useful because it gives you a very large sample size and shows that the issue is not only about memory, but also about regimen complexity and medication management systems.

Another major study, the REMIND randomized clinical trial, followed 53,480 patients taking one to three long-term oral medicines. It found that low-cost reminder devices did not significantly improve adherence overall, which is important because it shows that a simple reminder alone may not solve the problem. In the trial, the proportion achieving optimal adherence above 80% medication possession ratio was around 15.1% to 16.3% across groups, with no meaningful advantage over control.
What this means for your design research

The REMIND trial is especially useful because it shows that a medication aid needs more than just a physical reminder object. If users do not engage with the device consistently, or if the reminder is not tied to a stronger behavior system, the effect may be limited. This supports the idea that successful medication support should combine multiple functions rather than rely on a single prompt.

The study also suggests that reminder tools may work better when they are targeted to higher-risk users instead of being given to everyone in the same way. That is a strong justification for focusing on older adults and people with multiple medications, because they are more likely to need structured support.
Usability evidence you can add

A study on electronic medication adherence products examined usability and workload, showing that the user experience of these devices matters a lot in real life. This is useful for your project because a medication aid for older adults must be easy to understand, easy to refill, and not mentally tiring to operate. If a product feels too complicated, users may abandon it even if the idea is good.

Older adults have also reported positive experiences with dispensing devices when they are reliable and easy to use. One study found that older adults accepted a medication dispensing device as reliable, easy to use, and useful in coordinating personal medication management. This is valuable because it gives you evidence that the storage side of the problem can work well if the product is intuitive and supportive.
Evidence about what users need from reminder systems

Research on unobtrusive intelligent reminding found that reminders are more effective when they are delivered at an appropriate time rather than just randomly or loudly. That matters because timing is one of the biggest issues in medication adherence, especially where doses need to fit a daily routine. It suggests that a well-designed reminder system should focus on the right moment, not just the existence of an alarm.

The NHS guidance also supports this by saying reminders work better when they fit the user’s routine and are linked to everyday habits. Together, these sources point to the importance of scheduling logic, not just notification hardware.
Extra points for your analysis section
Summary

These extra studies help justify that the need is not just “people forget medicine.” It is also that many current solutions are too simple, too generic, or too hard to use consistently. That strengthens our design direction because it shows why a more structured, user-friendly medication support system is needed for older adults and people with multiple medicines.
Large studies show the problem affects tens of thousands of patients and is strongly linked to multiple medicines and chronic illness.
Simple reminder devices do not always improve adherence, so a stronger design needs more than one function.
Usability is critical because even good products may fail if users find them too difficult to set up or maintain.
Older adults value devices that feel reliable and easy to understand.
Reminder timing should be intelligent and routine-based rather than generic.

Survey Responses
Analysis of Research Data

The questionnaire and interviews revealed several common issues associated with medication management. The survey showed that 48% of respondents take three or more medicines daily, increasing the likelihood of confusion and mistakes. Additionally, 64% of respondents reported forgetting medication doses at least occasionally, indicating that medication adherence is a widespread problem.

The results also showed that while many respondents use phone alarms or other reminder methods, 36% still rely on memory alone, making them vulnerable to missed doses. Furthermore, 32% of respondents admitted to taking the wrong medicine or dosage at least once, highlighting the need for clearer medication identification and guidance.

A significant finding was that 46% of respondents found it difficult to distinguish between different medicines, while 82% believed that a screen displaying medicine names and timing would be useful. This suggests that users would benefit from a system that provides clear visual information regarding medication schedules and identification.

The survey also found strong support for reminder features. 80% of respondents considered audio reminders helpful, demonstrating the importance of using multiple reminder methods to attract user attention. In addition, 78% stated that confirming a dose before taking it was important, indicating that users value reassurance and verification before consuming medication.

The most common challenge identified was remembering medication timing, selected by 62% of respondents. Other significant issues included organizing medication schedules, remembering whether a dose had already been taken, and identifying medicines correctly.

The interview responses further reinforced these findings. Elderly participants reported problems with forgetfulness and distinguishing between similar-looking tablets. Working adults highlighted the impact of busy schedules on medication adherence, while caregivers emphasized the importance of monitoring and tracking medication intake.

The chosen design opportunity focuses on creating a system that reminds users when medication is due and clearly identifies the medicine that should be taken. By combining audio reminders, visual information, and organized medication storage, the design aims to reduce missed doses and medication errors .

Comparison
Conclusion :

Based on the comparison, storing tablets individually after removing them from their original blister packaging is the more suitable option for this product. blocks.text: Further Market Research of Potential End-Users

Following the development of the four initial concepts, further market research was carried out to determine which design would best meet the needs of the target users. The aim was to identify the most suitable concept and gather suggestions for refinement before producing the final design proposal.
Method
A concept evaluation questionnaire was conducted with 20 potential end-users.

Each participant was shown printed sketches of the four design concepts and a brief explanation of how each product operated. Participants were then asked to complete a questionnaire and discuss the strengths and weaknesses of each concept.

blocks.text: Conclusion

The additional market research confirmed that users valued simplicity, accessibility and reliability more than complex mechanisms. The drawer-based concept received the highest level of user acceptance (11 out of 20 participants) due to its ease of use, simple refilling process and clear medication organisation. Feedback also highlighted the importance of spoken reminders, a large confirmation button, a front-mounted display and a stable enclosure. These findings directly informed the refinement of the final design proposal, ensuring that it better satisfies the needs of elderly users, patients managing long-term medication and caregivers.
Removal of Drawer Numbering

The permanent numbering of the drawers was removed because it is not necessary for the user to identify the correct compartment. The product already incorporates multiple guidance features that clearly indicate which drawer needs to be opened. When medication is due, the OLED display shows the medication information and the required drawer, while the green LED positioned above the correct drawer illuminates to provide a clear visual indication. In addition, the audio reminder system provides an audible instruction identifying the required drawer.

Therefore, adding numbers to every drawer would provide duplicated information and could make the front of the product appear more cluttered. Removing the numbers creates a simpler, cleaner and more modern appearance, while still maintaining clear guidance for the user.

This is particularly beneficial for the intended elderly users because they do not need to remember which number corresponds to each medication. Instead, the product directly shows, lights and audibly identifies the required compartment.

blocks.text: Summary of Findings and Conclusions

The testing showed that the final medication management system successfully performed most of its intended functions. The eight drawers moved smoothly without sticking, and the drawer guides and stoppers worked correctly to keep the drawers aligned and prevent them from being removed accidentally. The main structure remained stable during use, and the joints were sufficiently strong for the intended application. The edges were also smoothed, reducing the risk of injury during normal operation.

The electronic system also performed successfully. The OLED displayed the current time and date accurately, while the DS3231 RTC maintained the time after being set. The individual drawer LEDs operated correctly, allowing the required drawer to be identified during a reminder. The confirmation button responded correctly, and the ESP32 was able to control the reminder sequence. The DFPlayer and speaker were also tested successfully for playing the required audio reminders.The medication scheduling and reminder system demonstrated that the product could identify the required medication and indicate the appropriate drawer at the scheduled time. The Blynk interface was able to communicate with the ESP32 and provide medication information.

Some limitations were identified during testing. The product was heavier than the expected 1.5 Kgs but however this could have been avoided if PETG was used.PETG was specified as the main material, but acrylic was used for the final prototype because PETG was unavailable. The final prototype also did not include separate power and charging indicator LEDs, so this part of the specification was only partially achieved. The battery capacity was within the intended range, but the full 5 to 7 day operating period would require longer-duration testing to confirm. Similarly, the expected 3 to 5 year lifespan could not be fully verified within the available testing period.

Overall, the testing demonstrated that the final product is functional, stable, safe to operate and suitable for its intended medication management purpose. The main functions, including medication reminders, drawer identification, time display, confirmation and electronic control, were successfully achieved. The remaining limitations mainly relate to material availability and long-term performance rather than the basic operation of the product. Therefore, the testing provides evidence that the final design is a practical working prototype, while further long-term testing and minor modifications could improve the finished product.
Further Improvements to the Product
Based on the testing and evaluation, the following improvements could be made:
Improvements to the individual one-off product

Reduce the overall weight: The finished product was relatively heavy. The structure could be made lighter by reducing unnecessary material thickness and using lighter materials where strength is not critical.(May have been avoided if PETG was used)
Use PETG instead of acrylic: PETG was specified for the final product but could not be sourced for the prototype. It would reduce weight while providing good durability and impact resistance.
Improve battery life: Use a more efficient power-management system and optimize the electronics to reduce power consumption.
Add separate status indicators: Add Power, Reminder and Charging LEDs to fully meet the original specification.
Improve the speaker: Use a slightly clearer speaker or improve the speaker enclosure so that audio reminders are easier to hear.
Reduce Material thickness : this will reduce the weight of the product.
Modifications for manufacturing in quantity
For producing 10 or more units, the design would need to be adapted for batch production:
Reduce the number of different parts: Combine or redesign some components where possible to simplify assembly.
Drawer front + drawer body
Drawer guide + stopper
Use PETG sheets: Purchase PETG in bulk to reduce material cost and ensure consistent material properties.
Design a custom PCB: Replace loose wires and individually connected components with a PCB containing the ESP32 connections, LED resistors and power connections.
Use connectors: Use standard connectors for the OLED, RTC, LEDs, speaker and other replaceable components to make assembly and maintenance easier.
Create assembly jigs: Use simple jigs to position the drawer guides, LEDs and panels consistently on every unit.
Batch-produce the drawers: Manufacture all drawers using the same dimensions and cutting process to ensure they slide correctly in every unit.
Quality control: Check dimensions, drawer movement, electronics, display, LEDs, audio, battery operation and software at each production stage.
Modular electronics: Make the electronics easy to replace so individual faulty components do not require the whole product to be replaced.
Evaluation of Materials, Tools and Equipment
Materials :

Acrylic: Acrylic was used for the one-off prototype because PETG was unavailable. It was easy to cut and assemble, but the finished product was relatively heavy. For batch production, PETG would be more suitable because it is lighter and durable.

Adhesive: Adhesive was suitable for permanently joining the acrylic components and was easy to use for the one-off product. For batch production, a suitable adhesive and controlled application method would be used to ensure that every joint has a consistent amount of adhesive.

Electronic components: The ESP32, OLED, RTC, LEDs, button and DFPlayer worked effectively in the prototype. For 10 or more products, these components could be purchased in bulk to reduce cost and ensure consistency.

Wiring: Individual wires and jumper wires were suitable for testing and making the one-off prototype, but they create a less organised assembly for quantity production. A custom PCB with connectors would be used instead to make wiring faster, neater and more reliable.
Tools and Equipment

Laser cutter: Suitable for accurately producing the acrylic panels in the one-off product. For a batch of 10, the same CAD files could be reused to cut identical panels, improving consistency and reducing production time.

Hand tools: Tools such as drills and screwdrivers were useful for finishing and assembling the prototype. For quantity production, jigs(for assembling) and more specialised equipment could be used to improve accuracy and speed.

Soldering equipment: A soldering iron was suitable for connecting the electronics in the one-off product. For 10 products, a standardised PCB would reduce the amount of individual soldering required and make assembly more consistent.

Measuring equipment: Rulers and measuring tools were suitable for checking the dimensions of the prototype. For batch production, more accurate measuring equipment could be used during quality control to ensure that all products meet the same dimensions.
CAD/CAM: CAD drawings would be reused to manufacture identical components for all 10 products. This would reduce errors and ensure consistency between products.

Purchasing PETG and electronic components in bulk.
Using the same CAD files to manufacture all components.
Using jigs to position the drawer guides and electronic components accurately.
Replacing loose wiring with a custom PCB and connectors.
Using a batch laser cutting process to produce identical components.

Evaluation of Wider Issues of Quantity Manufacturing

Moving from one-off production to a batch production would have cultural, social, economic and environmental impacts. Although producing in quantity would make the product more consistent and affordable, it would also increase the use of materials, energy and resources.
1. Cultural and Social Factors

rows.text: The dispenser could help elderly users and people who take several medicines manage their medication without constantly relying on a caregiver.
Some elderly users may find the electronic system or custom app difficult to understand, especially if they are not familiar with smartphones.
Producing more units would allow the product to be used by more families and could reduce the amount of time caregivers spend reminding users about medication.
Caregivers may still need to set up the app and medication schedules, creating an additional responsibility.
Batch production could make the product available to a larger number of people instead of being limited to one prototype.
The product may not suit every user's medication routine because the standardised design has a fixed number of compartments.
Producing 10 identical products means users receive the same layout, controls and operating system.
Mass-produced products have less opportunity for individual customisation compared with a one-off product.
The custom app and ESP32 system make the product more modern and could encourage users to use technology to manage their medication.
Users who do not own or regularly use a smartphone could find the system less convenient.

blocks.text: Evaluation: Overall, quantity production would have a positive social impact because the product could help more users manage their medication independently. However, the interface must remain simple, with clear instructions and large controls so that technology does not become a barrier for elderly users.
2. Economic Factors
Batch production would change the economics of the product significantly.
Advantages:
Buying PETG, electronic components and fasteners in larger quantities could reduce the cost per unit.
Producing 10 products using the same CAD files reduces design and preparation time for each product.
Using a custom PCB instead of individually connecting loose wires would reduce assembly time and improve consistency.
The same custom app can be digitally distributed to all 10 products, so it does not need to be developed separately for each dispenser.
Standardised parts make repairs and replacement easier.
A lower production cost could allow the product to be sold within the target price range of ₹4,000 to ₹8,000.
Disadvantages:
There would be a higher initial cost for purchasing materials and electronic components for 10 products.(Could be avoided by using Just in Time manufacturing )
Manufacturing equipment, electricity, PCB production and labour would increase the initial investment.
If demand is lower than expected, some finished products could remain unsold.
Developing the custom app requires additional programming and testing before the products can be sold.
Batteries and electronic components can increase the cost compared with a simple mechanical pillbox.

Evaluation: Batch production is economically more suitable than making each product individually because repeated manufacturing reduces the average production cost. However, the manufacturer would need to make sure there is enough demand to justify the initial investment.
3. Environmental Factors

rows.text: Producing 10 units creates more plastic waste from cutting and manufacturing.
Nest parts closely on sheets and reuse suitable offcuts.
Ten products require more ESP32 boards, PCBs, LEDs, displays and other electronic components.
Use replaceable modules and design the electronics so faulty parts can be repaired rather than replacing the whole product.
Each product requires rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, increasing the number of batteries eventually requiring responsible disposal.
Use rechargeable batteries with appropriate protection and make them replaceable.
CAD/CAM equipment, cutting, 3D printing/fabrication and electronics production use additional energy when producing 10 units.
Manufacture parts in batches to reduce repeated machine setup and minimise unnecessary production time.
Ten products require more packaging materials.
Use recyclable cardboard packaging and minimise unnecessary plastic packaging.
A durable PETG body and replaceable electronics could allow the product to last several years.
Design for repair and replacement of individual components.
Selling and transporting 10 products increases emissions compared with producing only one local prototype.
Batch transport and use local suppliers where possible.

blocks.text: Evaluation: The biggest environmental disadvantage is that quantity production increases the amount of PETG, electronics, batteries, packaging and energy used. However, designing the product for repair, reusing PETG offcuts, reducing packaging and manufacturing parts efficiently can reduce its environmental impact.
Overall Evaluation

Moving from a one-off production to batch production of 10 units would make the smart medication dispenser more commercially realistic. The main social benefit is that more elderly users and caregivers could benefit from a system that supports medication management. Economically, batch production would reduce the average cost through bulk purchasing, standardised parts and repeated manufacturing. However, the initial investment would be higher.

The main environmental concern is the increased consumption of PETG, electronic components, batteries and energy. This can be reduced through efficient material nesting, repairable electronics, recyclable packaging and responsible battery disposal.

Overall, batch production is appropriate for this product because the social and economic benefits can outweigh the disadvantages, provided that manufacturing is carefully planned to control cost, waste and environmental impact.
